title: “GREATER WORKS THAN THESE” — DID JESUS REALLY PROMISE CHRISTIANS GREATER MIRACLES THAN HIS?
paragraphs:
“GREATER WORKS THAN THESE” — DID JESUS REALLY PROMISE CHRISTIANS GREATER MIRACLES THAN HIS?
Jesus raised the dead, opened blind eyes, commanded storms, and walked on water. Then He looked at ordinary believers and said they would do “greater works.” What He meant may be far more astonishing—and far more personal—than the miracle-centered version many of us have heard.
There is a sentence Jesus spoke that can make an ordinary Christian feel strangely inadequate.
Maybe you have read it before.
Maybe you quietly skipped over it because you did not know what to do with it.
Maybe someone quoted it while preaching about supernatural power, healing, signs, wonders, prosperity, revival, or becoming a person through whom extraordinary miracles happen.
And somewhere inside you, a troubling question formed.
“If Jesus said believers would do greater works than He did…why doesn’t my life look like that?”
Jesus touched lepers.
You struggle to get through Monday.
Jesus opened blind eyes.
You have prayed for someone who remained sick.
Jesus commanded a storm to become silent.
You cannot always silence the storm inside your own mind.
Jesus fed thousands with a handful of food.
Jesus walked across the sea.
Jesus called Lazarus out of a tomb after four days.
Then, on the night before the cross, He said something breathtaking:
“Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father.”
John 14:12.
Read that last phrase again.
“Greater works than these.”
The Greek reads:
“καὶ μείζονα τούτων ποιήσει”
kai meizona toutōn poiēsei.
“And greater than these he will do.”
The word translated “greater” is μείζονα — meizona, the comparative form of megas: greater, larger, more significant.
And yes…
Jesus really said it.
We do not need to weaken His words.
But we also must not rip them away from the sentence that explains them.
Because Jesus did not stop after saying “greater works.”
He immediately said:
“ὅτι ἐγὼ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα πορεύομαι”
hoti egō pros ton patera poreuomai.
“Because I am going to the Father.”
That “because” matters.
It may be the word that rescues this entire passage from one of its most common misunderstandings.
Jesus did not say believers would perform greater works because they would eventually become more spiritually powerful than Jesus.
He did not say His disciples would graduate beyond their Master.
He did not announce that Christianity would produce generations of miracle workers who would individually outperform the incarnate Son of God.
The reason He gives is startlingly different:
“Because I am going to the Father.”
Something was about to happen.
Something enormous.
Jesus was going away.
But His departure was not defeat.
The cross was coming.
The resurrection was coming.
The ascension was coming.
The Holy Spirit was coming.
And the Gospel was about to explode beyond the geographical boundaries of Jesus’ earthly ministry into the nations of the world.
That changes everything.
Remember where John 14 occurs.
This is not Jesus speaking to an excited stadium crowd.
This is the shadow of the cross.
Judas has already gone into the night.
Jesus knows betrayal is moving toward Him.
Peter’s denial has been foretold.
His disciples are confused.
Their world is beginning to collapse.
And Jesus tells them:
“Let not your hearts be troubled.”
These are words spoken to frightened men who were about to watch their Messiah arrested, humiliated, tortured, and crucified.
Imagine sitting there.
They had left everything for Him.
They had watched demons flee.
They had watched bread multiply.
They had watched the dead rise.
They had watched storms obey His voice.
And now Jesus keeps talking about leaving.
Philip says, essentially, “Show us the Father.”
Jesus responds that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father. He tells them that the Father dwelling in Him does His works and calls them to believe because of the works themselves.
Then comes John 14:12.
The “works” are therefore not floating in isolation.
They belong to the revelation of who Jesus is and what the Father is accomplishing through Him.
And then Jesus says believers will continue His works—and do “greater” ones—because He is going to the Father.
Notice what happens after He goes.
A frightened fisherman stands in Jerusalem.
Peter.
The same Peter who denied knowing Jesus.
The same Peter who had once crumbled beside a charcoal fire when someone questioned him.
Now he stands publicly and proclaims the crucified and risen Christ.
And Acts 2 records something extraordinary.
About three thousand people receive the message and are baptized.
Think about that.
Jesus had ministered publicly for years.
Crowds followed Him.
Crowds abandoned Him.
Some worshiped.
Some doubted.
Some wanted His miracles without wanting His lordship.
Some shouted “Hosanna” and later Jerusalem would hear cries for crucifixion.
Yet after Christ's death, resurrection, ascension, and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, the Gospel begins spreading with breathtaking force.
Jerusalem.
Judea.
Samaria.
Then outward.
Across languages.
Across cultures.
Across borders.
Across centuries.
Eventually, the name of Jesus would be proclaimed in places those first disciples could barely have imagined.
This is why “greater” should not automatically be reduced to “more spectacular miracles.”
Consider the problem with that interpretation.
What exactly would “greater miracles than Jesus” mean?
Jesus gave sight to the blind.
Would greater mean giving someone two additional eyes?
Jesus multiplied bread for thousands.
Would greater mean feeding twenty thousand?
Jesus walked on water.
Would greater mean running across an ocean?
Jesus raised Lazarus after four days.
Would someone need to raise a person after five days to qualify?
That quickly turns Jesus’ words into a spiritual competition He never created.
And Christianity becomes obsessed with spectacle.
Who healed the most?
Who had the biggest meeting?
Who performed the most dramatic sign?
Who can tell the most unbelievable testimony?
Suddenly Jesus becomes the benchmark Christians are supposed to outperform rather than the Lord they are supposed to glorify.
But listen to Jesus’ own purpose in the very next verse.
He speaks about asking in His name and says the purpose is:
“ἵνα δοξασθῇ ὁ πατὴρ ἐν τῷ υἱῷ”
hina doxasthē ho patēr en tō huiō.
“So that the Father may be glorified in the Son.”
John 14:13.
There is the center.
Not us.
Not our reputation.
Not our spiritual résumé.
Not the size of our platform.
Not whether people walk away saying, “What a powerful Christian.”
The Father glorified in the Son.
Jesus remains the center.
This does not mean miracles stopped mattering.
Acts contains genuine signs and wonders.
The apostles heal the sick.
Peter and John encounter a man unable to walk, and he rises.
Extraordinary miracles accompany portions of the apostolic mission.
God remains completely sovereign and capable of miraculous intervention.
Christians are right to pray boldly.
We should pray for healing.
We should pray for deliverance.
We should pray believing God can do what human beings cannot.
But there is a profound difference between believing God performs miracles and believing John 14:12 promises every Christian a ministry of miracles more spectacular than Jesus’.
The verse says neither that every believer will reproduce every miracle Jesus performed nor that every faithful Christian must become individually more spectacular than Christ.
The emphasis falls somewhere deeper.
Jesus is returning to the Father.
The Spirit will be given.
The witnesses of Christ will carry His Gospel outward.
And through ordinary, weak, sometimes frightened people, the risen Christ will continue His mission on a scale His earthly ministry intentionally did not pursue before the cross.
This is where the verse suddenly becomes uncomfortable again.
Because perhaps you have been waiting for “greater works” to mean something dramatic enough to make people notice you.
But Jesus may be inviting you into something that makes people notice Him.
There is a miracle the world desperately needs to see.
A proud man becoming humble.
A bitter woman forgiving.
A secret sinner finally stepping into the light.
A husband confessing what he has hidden.
A wife choosing grace instead of revenge.
An addict crying out to Christ.
A lukewarm Christian falling to his knees in repentance.
A wounded believer refusing to let suffering turn into hatred.
A father finally saying, “I was wrong.”
A son returning home.
A person who spent years running from God whispering through tears:
“Jesus…save me.”
Do not misunderstand this.
Conversion is not a human accomplishment.
Only God saves.
Only Christ's blood atones.
Only the Spirit gives life.
No evangelist can resurrect a spiritually dead heart by eloquence.
No preacher can manipulate someone into the kingdom.
No Christian can boast that he saved anybody.
That is precisely what makes Gospel ministry so astonishing.
God chooses to place His treasure in jars of clay.
People like us.
Cracked people.
People with histories.
People with regrets.
People who have cried in bathrooms where nobody could hear.
People who have deleted browser histories.
People who have smiled in church while quietly falling apart.
People who have promised God, “Never again,” and then failed again.
People who sometimes wonder whether Jesus could possibly still want them.
And perhaps that is you.
Maybe the question that brought you into this article was theological:
“Did Jesus really promise greater miracles?”
But somewhere along the way another question started following you.
“Could Jesus still do something with me?”
After everything?
After the compromise?
After the secret?
After the years you wasted?
After what you became?
After the prayer life that disappeared?
After the Bible gathered dust?
After the affair?
After the addiction?
After the anger?
After the hypocrisy?
After the night nobody knows about?
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that respectable people can improve themselves.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Jesus did not merely come to demonstrate supernatural power.
He came to save.
The hands that opened blind eyes were eventually pierced.
The feet that walked on water were nailed to wood.
The One who called Lazarus out of his tomb entered death Himself.
And unlike Lazarus, Jesus did not rise merely to die again someday.
Christ conquered the grave.
That is the scandal.
The innocent One condemned.
The Holy One bearing sin.
The King wearing thorns.
The Creator mocked by His creatures.
The Son of God crucified between criminals.
And then…
grace.
The tomb opens.
Death loses its claim.
The risen Christ commissions His witnesses.
The Spirit comes.
The Gospel moves.
Sinners repent.
Enemies become family.
Persecutors become preachers.
The ashamed become witnesses.
The broken become vessels.
And generation after generation, the message keeps traveling.
That is what “greater works” looks like when Jesus remains at the center.
Not Christians becoming greater than Christ.
Christ continuing His work through His people after returning to the Father.
The greatness belongs to Him.
The power belongs to Him.
The Gospel belongs to Him.
The glory belongs to Him.
And perhaps the greatest correction some of us need is painfully simple:
Stop asking, “How can I become impressive enough for God to use me?”
Start asking, “Jesus, how can my life make You known?”
Because maybe your “greater work” will never trend.
Maybe nobody will put your testimony on a stage.
Maybe you will never preach to thousands.
Maybe you will never see a miracle that makes strangers pull out their phones.
Maybe your obedience looks like opening Scripture with your children tonight.
Maybe it means forgiving someone who will never apologize.
Maybe it means confessing your sin instead of protecting your image.
Maybe it means sharing Christ with one coworker who thinks Christianity is ridiculous.
Maybe it means praying with the person everybody else abandoned.
Maybe it means returning to church after years of shame.
Maybe it means refusing pornography tonight.
Maybe it means telling your spouse the truth.
Maybe it means finally surrendering the part of your life you keep telling Jesus He cannot touch.
Nobody may applaud.
Heaven does not need applause.
Faithfulness does not become insignificant simply because it is invisible.
And there is another danger hiding inside our obsession with miracles.
We can want the works of Jesus while secretly wanting the fame of Jesus.
We can want power without holiness.
Anointing without repentance.
Influence without obedience.
Crowds without crosses.
Resurrection power without dying to self.
We can shout about “greater works” while refusing the simplest command Christ gave us yesterday.
That should disturb us.
Because the Christian life is not a quest to become spiritually impressive.
It is surrender to a crucified and risen King.
So be honest.
What if the greatest miracle you need right now is not something happening around you?
What if it needs to happen inside you?
Not because regeneration or sanctification makes you the hero.
Quite the opposite.
Because when Christ transforms the person everybody thought would never change—including the person staring back at you from the mirror—Jesus gets the glory.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Maybe everyone thinks you are doing fine.
You know the Christian vocabulary.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know what worship songs to play.
You know what verses to post.
But underneath the Christian appearance is exhaustion.
Or compromise.
Or anger.
Or unbelief.
Or a secret sin slowly eating the inside of your life.
You do not need another performance.
You need Christ.
Not Christianity as decoration.
Christ.
Not religious content.
Christ.
Not another emotional moment you forget tomorrow morning.
Christ.
The Jesus who died for sinners.
The Jesus who rose from the grave.
The Jesus who calls people to repent and believe.
The Jesus who receives the brokenhearted but refuses to leave us enslaved to the very sins destroying us.
The Jesus who forgives.
The Jesus who restores.
The Jesus who rewrites stories.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not manufacture a dramatic response for other people.
Just be honest.

And if Christ has already been rewriting your story, tell somebody what He has done. Your testimony does not have to make you look impressive. In fact, perhaps the most powerful testimony is the one where Jesus clearly receives all the credit.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person who has struggled.
Someone may need your honesty more than your image of perfection.
And someone on your Facebook friends list may never walk into a church this week.
But they might read something you share.
That matters.
Send it privately to the believer who has been measuring God's love by whether their prayers produced spectacular miracles.
“Because I am going to the Father.”
We want people opening Scripture.
Testing claims.
Asking difficult questions.
Repenting where Scripture confronts us.
Resting in grace where the Gospel comforts us.
Growing deeper in Jesus rather than merely consuming more Christian content.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It cannot.
Not because you must pay Gospel Warrior in order to glorify God.
Scripture teaches no such thing.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives of grateful obedience to Him.
But one expression of that obedience can be voluntarily supporting faithful Gospel work and helping sound biblical resources reach more people.
Jesus is not selling you access to Himself.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness cannot be purchased.
The blood of Christ cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift received through faith in Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is the final surprise hidden inside “greater works.”
The verse was never permission to make Christianity about us.
It was always pulling our eyes toward what Christ would accomplish after going to the Father.
The crucified Jesus would rise.
The risen Jesus would ascend.
The ascended Jesus would send the Spirit.
The Spirit-empowered church would bear witness.
The Gospel would cross borders.
Sinners would hear.
People would believe.
Lives would change.
And two thousand years later, somewhere far beyond first-century Jerusalem, someone would be staring at a screen reading the words of Jesus.
Maybe with tears.
Maybe with questions.
Maybe after years of running.
Maybe after another failure.
Maybe wondering whether grace could possibly reach this far.
It can.
Not because your story is clean.
Because His cross is enough.
Not because you performed greater miracles.
Because Jesus accomplished the work you could never accomplish for yourself.
Not because you finally became worthy.
Because Christ is worthy.
So stop trying to become the hero of your redemption.
You already have one.
His name is Jesus.
Share His Gospel.
Speak His name.
Love the forgotten.
Pray boldly.
Obey quietly.
Repent quickly.
Forgive freely.
Serve faithfully.
And when God does something extraordinary through your ordinary life, resist the temptation to turn the spotlight toward yourself.
Point it back where Jesus pointed it:
to the Father glorified in the Son.
Because someday the greatest testimony of your life may not be, “Look what I did for Jesus.”
It may simply be:
“Look what Jesus did with someone like me.”
The miracle was never that you became greater than Jesus. The miracle is that Jesus was willing to take your broken story and make it point back to Him.
